# Breton Civil War (1341–1343)

The **Breton Civil War (1341–1343)**, also known as the **War of the Breton Succession** or the **War of the Two Jeannes**, was a succession conflict in the Duchy of Brittany that arose following the death of Duke John III on April 30, 1341 . The war pitted two rival claimants—John of Montfort, the duke's half-brother, and Joan of Penthièvre, the duke's niece—against each other for control of the duchy . The conflict quickly became entangled in the broader Hundred Years' War between England and France, with King Philip VI supporting Joan and Charles of Blois while King Edward III backed John of Montfort .

The war's initial phase was marked by rapid developments, including John of Montfort's capture and imprisonment in November 1341, followed by his wife Joan of Montfort's remarkable resistance against Charles of Blois's forces . The conflict reached its peak in 1342 with several major military engagements, including the siege of Hennebont and the battle of Morlaix . The war ended inconclusively with the signing of the Truce of Malestroit on January 19, 1343, which temporarily halted hostilities while the succession question remained unresolved .

## Background and Succession Crisis

The Duchy of Brittany was a semi-autonomous province within the Kingdom of France, with its own distinct customs and traditions . Duke John III, who ruled from 1312 until his death on April 30, 1341, left no legitimate children despite three marriages . This succession crisis created a power vacuum that would plunge Brittany into civil war.

The two primary claimants to the duchy had equally valid claims under different legal interpretations. Joan of Penthièvre was the daughter of Guy, Duke John's younger brother, who had died in 1331 . In 1337, Duke John had married Joan to Charles of Blois, a nephew of King Philip VI of France . John of Montfort, meanwhile, was Duke John's half-brother, the son of Duke Arthur II by a second marriage .

The succession dispute was complicated by conflicting legal traditions. Brittany had historically allowed female succession, as evidenced by practices in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries before Brittany attained peerage status . However, John of Montfort argued that as a peerage of the French realm, Brittany should follow the same succession practices that governed the French kingship, which explicitly excluded women .

Duke John himself appeared to favor each claimant at different times. While he was generally explicit about his distaste for John of Montfort during most of his rule, Montfort claimed that the duke had reconciled with him three years after Joan's marriage to Charles of Blois . The chronicler Guillaume de Nangis reported that Duke John had even proposed to sell the duchy to Philip VI "in order to avoid the dangers which would befall the kingdom should the duchy fall into the hands of a woman," but this plan was opposed by certain Bretons and ultimately came to nothing .

## The Outbreak of War (1341)

Following Duke John's death, the rival claimants initially agreed to submit their dispute to King Philip VI for resolution. The French king convened a council at Conflans that met in September 1341. On September 7, the council issued a judgment in favor of Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois .

However, John of Montfort refused to accept the decision. According to chroniclers, he made a dramatic escape from the Parisian court and returned to Brittany in September 1341 . Upon his return, he seized the ducal treasury at Limoges and began assembling forces to press his claim through military means .

Charles of Blois and King Philip VI responded swiftly. In November 1341, they launched a campaign that culminated in the capture of John of Montfort at Nantes . The chronicler Jean Froissart later described how Montfort was taken prisoner and sent to Paris, where he would remain imprisoned for the next four years .

The imprisonment of John of Montfort might have ended the conflict immediately, but for the remarkable actions of his wife, Joan of Montfort. Upon learning of her husband's capture, she immediately took steps to secure the treasury, moving it to the castle of Brest under the guard of Tanguy of Chastel . She then emerged as the visible head of the Montfortist party in Brittany, rallying supporters and preparing for the inevitable French assault.

## Joan of Montfort's Resistance (1341–1342)

Joan of Montfort's leadership during this critical period has been noted by chroniclers for its military and political sophistication. Contemporary accounts describe her as having "the heart of a man and a lion" . She proved herself to be a capable military commander and diplomat, performing tasks that were traditionally reserved for the male half of the noble couple.

In March 1342, Joan sent a letter to the people of Saint-Malo, promising to safeguard their town and goods by both sea and land . This document represents one of the few surviving pieces of direct evidence of her activities during this period. The letter demonstrates her commitment to military action and her recognition of the need to protect key coastal towns that remained loyal to the Montfortist cause.

By early 1342, Charles of Blois had assembled a substantial army. According to chroniclers, his forces included 5,000 French soldiers, 2,000 Genoese mercenaries, and a large but unknown number of Breton soldiers . With this army, he began a systematic campaign to eliminate the remaining Montfortist strongholds.

## The Siege of Hennebont (1342)

One of the most dramatic episodes of the war occurred in May-June 1342 with the siege of Hennebont, a fortified port town in southern Brittany. Joan of Montfort had taken refuge there with her supporters, including members of the Clisson family, notably Amaury of Clisson .

The siege began when Charles of Blois's forces surrounded the town, cutting off all supply routes and launching assaults against its defenses. Joan of Montfort's leadership during this siege has been particularly celebrated in historical accounts. According to Froissart, she rallied the women and children inside the town, urging them to tear stones from the streets to use as ammunition against the attacking forces .

The most famous incident occurred when Joan devised a daring plan to break the siege. She armed herself and mounted a warhorse, leading a small group of men behind the enemy lines. Under cover of darkness, they set fire to the French camp, which was poorly guarded. The resulting confusion allowed her to lead her foes on a fruitless chase away from the town . She returned the next day to rally her troops and townspeople, who continued to hold out until help arrived.

The arrival of English reinforcements in June 1342 finally lifted the siege. A force of 234 men under Sir Walter Mauny, a member of Edward III's household, managed to penetrate the Blavet River (present-day Port-Louis) and relieve the besieged town . This marked the beginning of direct English military intervention in the Breton Civil War.

## English Intervention and the Campaign of 1342

The English had been watching developments in Brittany with increasing interest. King Edward III saw an opportunity to establish a friendly ruler in Brittany who would provide access to Breton ports, greatly aiding England's naval war against France and offering a ready entry point for English armies into France .

The first significant English force arrived in May 1342 under Sir Walter Mauny. His small contingent of 234 men successfully relieved Hennebont, where Joan of Montfort was being besieged . This initial success encouraged Edward III to plan a larger expedition.

The Earl of Northampton was appointed to command the first major contingent of the English army, consisting of 1,350 men, with orders to sail from Portsmouth on July 8, 1342. However, the English faced significant logistical challenges. On the appointed date, not a single requisitioned ship was present . Through threats and confiscations, the English eventually assembled a fleet of 440 ships, but even this would require multiple trips to transport the 6,000 men Edward wished to deploy.

By July, the military situation had deteriorated significantly for the Montfortist cause. Joan of Montfort had been forced back to the far west of Brittany and was besieged in the port of Brest, the only remaining fortified place still held by her faction . Charles of Blois had captured most of the major towns, including Auray, Vannes, and Hennebont ).

The English fleet finally sailed on August 14-15, 1342, with 140 transports and 120 warships. They arrived off Brest on August 18, just as the town was on the verge of surrender. The English fleet took the Genoese ships blockading the port by surprise, defeated them, and burned most of their vessels .

The arrival of the English fleet had an immediate impact on the strategic situation. Charles of Blois, seeing the large number of English ships and assuming a vast army had arrived, promptly broke off the siege of Brest and withdrew 70 miles to Guingamp . There he concentrated his forces and called up local levies to prepare for the coming English invasion.

## Edward III's Campaign in Brittany (1342–1343)

Edward III himself arrived in Brittany on October 26, 1342, after a storm-wracked three-week passage from England. His army was much smaller than planned—fewer than 5,500 men—due to the difficulties in assembling shipping . The king had been forced to abandon his siege train on the beach at Sandwich and sail with only those troops he could fit on the available vessels.

Upon landing, Edward held a council of war with his commanders and the remaining Montfortist leaders. It was decided to march on Vannes, the second most populous settlement in Brittany, which had a good harbor and strong walls. From Vannes, the English could control much of southern Brittany .

The English army marched unopposed through southern Brittany for 120 miles, halting 12 miles from Vannes to construct siege engines—replacements for those left behind in England. On November 29, they attempted to take the town by storm, but the newly reinforced French garrison successfully repelled the assault, and a siege began .

While the main English force besieged Vannes, raiding parties were sent out to devastate large parts of eastern Brittany. The Earl of Salisbury led an expedition that razed the outskirts of Dinan and devastated the area around Dol, 100 miles northeast of Vannes . Other English forces captured Ploërmel, Malestroit, and Redon, and besieged Nantes, the ducal capital.

However, the English faced significant challenges. Their numbers were insufficient to maintain control of all the territory they had occupied, and the terms of service for many of their troops were running out. It is recorded that 400 Welsh archers left the army on December 17, 1342, because their contracts had expired .

## The French Response and the Truce of Malestroit

King Philip VI responded to the English invasion by assembling a large army under his son John, Duke of Normandy. The French army gathered at Angers, the main supply center, and began a methodical advance westward .

The approach of the French army created a tense situation. Edward III, despite his outward confidence, was alarmed by the size of the French force and the precarious position of his own army. He invited two cardinals who had been sent by Pope Clement VI to attempt a settlement to come to Malestroit, 18 miles from his camp .

The French advance was rapid. On Christmas Day 1342, they relieved Nantes, just in time to foil a plot to open the gates to the English . In early January 1343, they recaptured Redon, Ploërmel, and Malestroit, and established their camp around the latter.

Negotiations between the two sides intensified. Philip VI established his court at Redon and sent emissaries to the cardinals at Malestroit. By January 19, 1343, the terms of a truce had been agreed upon and were sealed in the Chapelle de la Madeleine at Malestroit .

The **Truce of Malestroit** was remarkable for its terms, which historian Jonathan Sumption described as "astonishingly favorable" to the English . The truce was to last until September 29, 1346, and both sides were to retain the territory they held at the time of the truce's signing . This meant that:

* The English would garrison the fortified places they held in Brittany

* Vannes would be held by the papacy for the duration of the truce

* Philip VI would immediately free John of Montfort

* There would be a general exchange of prisoners

John of Montfort was released from prison in September 1343 and retired to England, where he remained until March 27, 1345 . Edward III returned to England, arriving on March 1, 1343, after enduring another storm that scattered his fleet and sank several ships .

## Aftermath and Legacy

The Truce of Malestroit brought an end to the intense phase of the Breton Civil War (1341–1343), but it did not resolve the underlying succession dispute. The war would continue in a more sporadic fashion until 1364, when it was finally settled by the battle of Auray, in which Charles of Blois was killed .

The truce was short-lived in practice. Despite its three-and-a-half year duration, both sides began preparations for renewed hostilities almost immediately. The English garrisoned their positions in Brittany, with Brest remaining in English hands for the next 30 years . Late in 1343, Montfortist partisans in Vannes rose against the papal authority, expelled the garrison, and delivered the town to the English, who held it until the end of the war in 1364 .

The French, meanwhile, executed several Breton lords who were accused of supporting the English. Olivier IV de Clisson was executed in Paris on August 2, 1343, and on November 29, fourteen Breton lords were executed without trial, including Geoffroi de Malestroit, Jean de Montauban, and Alain de Quédillac .

The Breton Civil War had significant implications for the broader Hundred Years' War. It demonstrated the importance of Brittany as a strategic prize and showed how local disputes could draw in the major powers of Europe. The war also highlighted the changing role of women in medieval warfare, as both Joan of Montfort and Joan of Penthièvre demonstrated remarkable military and political capabilities.

The war finally ended in 1365 with the signing of the first Treaty of Guérande, which established John IV (the son of John of Montfort and Joan of Montfort) as the legitimate heir to the Duchy of Brittany . John IV subsequently signed a treaty of alliance with England, ensuring that Brittany would remain a valuable ally of England for the duration of the Hundred Years' War.

The Breton Civil War (1341–1343) thus represents a pivotal moment in medieval European history, demonstrating how personal ambitions, legal disputes, and international rivalries could combine to create prolonged conflict. The war's resolution would shape the political landscape of western France for centuries to come.

Truce of Malestroit
-------------------

[![Image 2: Commemorative plaque on the ruins of the , reading: "Historic ruins of the Magdalene chapel, where was signed on 19th. January 1343 during the Hundred Years' war by representatives of the English and French realms, the Truce of Malestroit, in the presence of Papal legates the Cardinals of Clermont and of Prenets](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG/250px-Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2d/Malestroit_-_Chapelle_de_la_Madeleine_plaque.JPG)

Commemorative plaque on the ruins of the Chapel of the Madeleine, reading: "Historic ruins of the Magdalene chapel, where was signed on 19th. January 1343 during the Hundred Years' war by representatives of the English and French realms, the Truce of Malestroit, in the presence of Papal legates the Cardinals of Clermont and of Prenets."

The **Truce of Malestroit** was signed on 19 January 1343 between [Edward III of England](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") and [Philip VI of France](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), in the chapelle de la Madeleine in Malestroit. After the signing of this truce, the English sovereign and his troops left Bretagne for England.

Scheduled to last only until 29 September, the truce was short-term; as of February Edward III ordered preparations for embarkation of military forces from Portsmouth. At this point the French king, Philippe VI, put an end to the truce by executing without trial (and despite prior agreements) Olivier IV de Clisson in Paris on 2 August, and then on 29 November a further fourteen Breton lords; Geoffroi de Malestroit, Jean de Montauban, Alain de Quédillac, Denis du Plessis, Guillaume II des Brieux and his brothers Jean and Olivier, and others. These were all supporters of Jean of Montfort. Even so, hostilities did not officially recommence till 1345; they were however pursued till 1362.

Targa commemorativa sulle rovine della Cappella di La Madeleine, con su scritto: "Rovine storica della cappella di Maddalena, dove fu firmata il 19 gennaio 1343 durante la guerra dei cent'anni da rappresentanti dei regni inglesi e francesi, la tregua di Malestroit, in presenza dei legati papali, i cardinali di Clermont e di Prenets."

La **tregua di Malestroit** fu firmata il 19 gennaio 1343 tra [Edoardo III d'Inghilterra](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edoardo_III_d'Inghilterra "Edoardo III d'Inghilterra") e [Filippo VI di Francia](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_VI_di_Francia "Filippo VI di Francia"), nella cappella di La Madeleine a [Malestroit](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit"). Dopo aver firmato la tregua, il sovrano inglese e le sue truppe lasciarono la [Bretagna](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretagna "Bretagna") per tornare in [Inghilterra](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inghilterra "Inghilterra").

La tregua, programmata per durare solo fino al 29 settembre, era di breve termine; a febbraio Edoardo III ordinò i preparativi per l'imbarco di forze militari da [Portsmouth](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth "Portsmouth"). A quel punto il re francese, Filippo VI, pose fine alla tregua, giustiziando senza processo (e nonostante precedenti accordi) [Olivier IV de Clisson](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_IV_de_Clisson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Olivier IV de Clisson (la pagina non esiste)") a [Parigi](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parigi "Parigi") il 2 agosto, e poi il 29 novembre quattordici lord bretoni: Geoffroi de Malestroit, Jean de Montauban, Alain de Quédillac, Denis du Plessis, Guillaume II des Brieux e i suoi fratelli Jean e Olivier, e altri. Furono tutti sostenitori di [Giovanni IV di Bretagna](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_IV_di_Bretagna "Giovanni IV di Bretagna"). Nonostante ciò, le ostilità non ricominciarono ufficialmente fino al 1345; furono perseguite fino al 1362.

Repères chronologiques de la guerre de Succession de Bretagne (1341-1365)
=========================================================================

 Auteur : [Laurence Moal](http://bcd.bzh/becedia/fr/laurence-moal) / septembre 2020 

**1341-1343: phase intense**
----------------------------

**Mort de Jean III:** Début de la guerre de Succession

**7 septembre 1341:** L’arrêt de Conflans donne raison à Jeanne de Penthièvre.

**Novembre 1341:** Capture de Montfort à Nantes et son emprisonnement à Paris

**1342:** Siège d’Hennebont

Débarquement à Brest des Anglais

Campagnes anglaise et française dans le duché

**1343-1362: phase de l’enlisement**
------------------------------------

**Janvier 1343:** L’Angleterre et la France concluent la trêve de Malestroit qui met fin aux hostilités durant deux ans

**1343:** Édouard III en Bretagne

Exécutions de seigneurs bretons accusés d’appuyer l’Angleterre

**1344:** Prise de Quimper et massacre de la population par Charles de Blois

**1345:** Libération de Jean de Montfort qui fait hommage à Édouard III

**1346:** Bataille de Crécy

**1347:** Bataille de La Roche-Derrien, capture de Blois et son transfert en Angleterre

Calais prise par les Anglais. Création de l’ordre de la Jarretière

**1349:**Olivier de Clisson rejoint Jean IV en Angleterre

**1351:**[Combat des Trente](http://bcd.bzh/becedia/fr/le-combat-des-trente)

Fin de la trêve entre la France et l’Angleterre

**1352:**Défaite à Mauron de l’élite française des chevaliers de l’ordre de l’Étoile

**1356:** Libération de Charles de Blois contre rançon

Défaite de Poitiers, captivité de Jean II le Bon

**1356-1357:** Défense de Rennes où s’illustre [Du Guesclin](http://bcd.bzh/becedia/fr/la-bretagne-de-du-guesclin-un-age-d-or)

**1358:**Pourparlers de Londres

**1359:**Rupture des négociations entre la France et l’Angleterre

Chevauchée d’Édouard III en Île-de-France

**1360:**Traité de Brétigny

**1361:** Réunion de Saint-Omer

Mort de Marguerite d’Angleterre (première épouse de Jean de Montfort, futur Jean IV)

**1362-1364: les prétendants face à face**
------------------------------------------

**1362:** Retour en Bretagne de Jean de Montfort

**1363:**Tentative de règlement négocié passant par un partage du duché à Évran

[Du Guesclin](http://bcd.bzh/becedia/fr/la-bretagne-de-du-guesclin-un-age-d-or) envoyé en Bretagne

**1364:** Mort de Jean le Bon à Londres. Sacre de Charles V

**29 septembre 1364:**[Bataille d’Auray](http://bcd.bzh/becedia/fr/la-bataille-dauray)

The **Battle of Champtoceaux**, often called the **Battle of l'Humeau**, was the opening action of the 23-year-long [Breton War of Succession](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession"), a dynastic conflict in Brittany which became inevitably embroiled in the [Hundred Years War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Hundred_Years_War "Hundred Years War") between England and France. The battle should have decided the war at a stroke, as the leader of one faction Jean de Montfort was made prisoner. His wife [Joanna of Flanders](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Joanna_of_Flanders "Joanna of Flanders") and son young John escaped imprisonment. Their escape and continued support from his ally, England, allowed continued resistance to flourish and eventually turn the tide.

*   [2 Charles' advance](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#Charles'_advance)

    *   [2.2 Siege of Nantes](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#Siege_of_Nantes)

Dynastic Conflict[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The [Breton War of Succession](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") was highly political and revolved around conflicting claims. The dynastic conflict over the Duchy of Brittany followed the death of John III, Duke of Brittany on April 30, 1341. His inheritance was claimed by two members of the Breton House of Dreux, his half brother John de Montfort and his niece Joan. Joan's husband, Charles of Blois, was the nephew of King Philip VI of France. The French king was bound to support his nephew's claim by the politic of family dynastics in medieval Europe. He was not, however, prepared to endure an expanded war on the distant Breton peninsula. Brittany at this time was a foreign land where travel was fraught with difficulties and the language alien. Philip VI encouraged John and Charles to come to terms on the succession. At this stage, Edward III, King of England stepped into the conflict offering troops and financial support to John de Montfort in exchange for homage from John for the ownership of Brittany. If successful, Edward III would thereby confirm Edward's claim to be the rightful ruler of France. Ironically, in supporting John whose claim to the ducal throne rested on salic law, Edward was jeopardising his own claim to the throne of France which deliberately ignored the same laws. The idea of English troops rampaging through Brittany and from there into [Normandy](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") and other parts of Northern France terrified Philip and he resolved to win the war before Edward's troops could arrive. John too was not idle, took flight from Paris days before his arrest for treason with Edward III; he and arrived in Nantes to raise an army from his supporters.

Charles' advance[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By the end of September 1341, Charles of Blois had 5,000 French soldiers, 2,000 Genoese mercenaries and an unknown but large number of Breton soldiers in his army. He encamped his army at Angers in the Loire Valley. [[lower-alpha 1]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-1)[[lower-alpha 2]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-2) By the time Charles de Blois was ready to move at the start of October 1341, Montfort had captured and garrisoned most of the castles and towns in Eastern Brittany. Montfort's castle strongholds included the towns of Rennes, Dinan and numerous others including the fortified castle (_chateau fort_) [[lower-alpha 3]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-3) which guarded the Loire Valley at Champtoceaux.[[lower-alpha 4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-4)[[lower-alpha 5]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-5) Blois made this stronghold the first objective of the French army as they marched towards their eventual target, Nantes. [[lower-alpha 6]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-6) Charles of Blois arrived near the castle on the 10 October with part of his army and laid siege to it before the remainder of the force arrived. This army was moving more slowly but its presence was already causing a number of John's supporters alarm. Mindful of the speed with which supporters disappeared in medieval dynastic struggles, John was forced to act, scraping together a band of followers and riding to the relief of Champtoceaux.

### Battle of Champtoceaux[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The attempted relief of Champtoceaux was a disaster for John de Montfort. His forces were strung out in a dozen garrisons and thus he cold only scrape a handful of men from Nantes to join his forces for this particular effort. This force was not big enough to challenge Charles' vanguard and was dwarfed by the large French army behind him. John could not expect English reinforcements in Brittany before the New Year. John halted at a small farmstead named l'Humeau, three miles from Champtoceaux, expecting it to be garrisoned by a small body of his supporters who could inform him of Charles' positions. To their mutual shock, he found Charles himself and almost overwhelmed his bodyguard. Charles barricaded himself in the farmhouse's tower and defeated all efforts by John's men to break in. For two days the two rivals engaged each other in the surreal circumstances; repeated efforts to gain access by John were driven off by Charles' defensive position. Meanwhile the French army crawled ever closer. Supporters of John came to aid him and a series of bloody and confused skirmishes occurred around the head of the French column; these skirmishes failed to blunt the steady progress of Blois' army towards Nantes.

### Siege of Nantes[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

Eventually John conceded defeat at Champtoceaux and rode as fast as he could for Nantes, pursued by French cavalry which had finally caught up with the action at l'Humeau. He had lost many of his supporters and mercenaries around Champtoceaux, which fell on the 26 October after the fact of John's flight became known. When he arrived at Nantes, he received a hostile reception from the townsmen who reacted to the defeat at Champtoceaux and the losses there; they agreed to support him further only if he promised them that he would surrender should no relief arrive for the city within a month. A series of sallies by the Montfortists followed in the coming days responded; the French army began its assaults on outlying forts held by John's forces. Captured defenders were executed by the French within sight of the city walls and discontent grew within the city to such a degree that John was having difficulty finding men to accompany his attacks on the French lines. Finally at the end of October a sally ended in disaster when John's mercenaries deserted at the height of battle and left the contingent of townsmen to be annihilated by a superior French force; some of the captured Montfortists were beheaded and their heads were thrown into the town with a catapult. John was forced to surrender on the 2 November by the irate city council and he was imprisoned in the Louvre in Paris.

Aftermath[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In quick succession, John's allies and holdings in Brittany disappeared either through desertion or direct assault by the French army . During the winter, Charles captured all of Eastern Brittany, and then in the spring most of Western Brittany. This left only the tiny port of Brest in the hands of Joanna of Flanders and a few English adventurers led by Walter Manny. It was at Brest in the [battle there](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_(1342) "Battle of Brest (1342)") in July 1342 that the promised English reinforcements finally arrived and the tide of war turned yet again and not for the last time. John de Montfort eventually escaped French custody in January 1345, dying a few months later. His infant son, raised in England, was still free and continued the war once he reached adulthood. John's son would eventually defeat Charles at the [Battle of Auray](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364, ending the war.

5.description: John of Montfort (in Breton Yann Moforzh, in French Jean de Montfort) (1295  16 September 1345, Chteau d'Hennebont), sometimes known as John IV, Duke of Brittany, and 6th Earl of Richmond from 1341 to his death. 5.content:
**John of Montfort** (in Breton **Yann Moñforzh**, in [French](https://alchetron.com/French-language)**Jean de Montfort**) (1295 – 16 September 1345, [Château d'Hennebont](https://alchetron.com/Hennebont)), sometimes known as **John IV, Duke of Brittany**, and 6th [Earl of Richmond](https://alchetron.com/Earl-of-Richmond) from 1341 to his death. He was the son of Arthur II, Duke of Brittany and his second wife, Yolande de Dreux. He contested the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany by his niece, Joan of Penthièvre, which led to the [War of the Breton Succession](https://alchetron.com/War-of-the-Breton-Succession), which in turn evolved into being part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://alchetron.com/Hundred-Years'-War) between England and France. John's patron in his quest was King [Edward III of England](https://alchetron.com/Edward-III-of-England). He died in 1345, 19 years before the end of the war, and the victory of his son John IV over Joan of Penthièvre and her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://alchetron.com/Charles%2C-Duke-of-Brittany).

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son to Arthur II of Brittany and his second wife Yolande of Dreux. In 1322 he inherited from his mother the title of [Count of Montfort](https://alchetron.com/Montfort-of-Brittany)-l'Amaury, and in 1329 he married [Joanna of Flanders](https://alchetron.com/Joanna-of-Flanders) in [Chartres](https://alchetron.com/Chartres). Joanna was the daughter of [Louis I, Count of Nevers](https://alchetron.com/Louis-I%2C-Count-of-Nevers), and [Joan, Countess of Rethel](https://alchetron.com/Joan%2C-Countess-of-Rethel). They had two children.

*   John IV, Duke of Brittany (1339–1399), married (1) [Mary of Waltham](https://alchetron.com/Mary-of-Waltham) (1344–1362), daughter of King [Edward III of England](https://alchetron.com/Edward-III-of-England), in 1361 in Oxfordshire; (2) [Joan Holland](https://alchetron.com/Joan-Holland%2C-Duchess-of-Brittany) (1350–1384) in 1366 in London; (3) [Joan of Navarre](https://alchetron.com/Joan-of-Navarre%2C-Queen-of-England) (1370–1437), daughter of King [Charles II of Navarre](https://alchetron.com/Charles-II-of-Navarre), in 1386 in Saillé-près-[Guérande](https://alchetron.com/Gu%C3%A9rande).
*   Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton (1341–1402), married before 21 October 1385 to Ralph Basset, 3rd Lord Basset of Drayton

On 30 April 1341, [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://alchetron.com/John-III%2C-Duke-of-Brittany), died without a male heir. His half-brother, John of Montfort, was a candidate for the succession, which was also claimed by Joan of Penthièvre, niece of John III and wife of Charles of Blois, himself a nephew of the [Philip VI, King of France](https://alchetron.com/Philip-VI-of-France). The King was, of course, favourable to his nephew.

The Duchy of Brittany historically had a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance; male primogeniture was followed unless no direct male descendants remained. At that point the closest female descendant inherited as Duchess, with her husband serving as Duke by "right of representation". The position of John of Montfort was legally founded on the belief that a brother (even a half-brother) was a closer heir than a beneficiary niece, and that the Salic form of inheritance adopted by the Kingdom of France should be followed. This argument was based on the fact that since 1297 Brittany had been a _Duché-pairie_ ("member and part of the crown"), and that the legislation of the suzerain kingdom should therefore be applied. Challenges to the [Salic law](https://alchetron.com/Salic-law) of the Franks had historically been rejected for the Kingdom of France, allowing Philip V to gain the throne in 1316, and Philip VI most recently. This made Edward III's support of John of Montfort quite ironic, in that the argument for Edward III to inherit the Kingdom of France was based on the opposing philosophy that the crown should be able to descend through a female line.

A civil war, termed the War of the Breton Succession, then began and lasted 23 years. This conflict was also called _La guerre de deux Jeanne_, after the French names of the two duchesses in competition: Jeanne de Penthièvre and Jeanne de Flanders, wife of John of Montfort.

After the funeral of John III, Charles of Blois returned to the Court of France and John of Montfort returned to his Breton estate in Guérande. Then, incited by his wife (according to tradition), he went with a small army to [Nantes](https://alchetron.com/Nantes) where he was well received by the inhabitants who swore their loyalty. John then went to [Limoges](https://alchetron.com/Limoges) where he managed to obtain the ducal treasury. John returned to [Nantes](https://alchetron.com/Nantes) and was recognised as Duke in May 1341 by an assembly composed of members of the towns and minor nobles, but shunned by the major vassals with the exception of Hervé VII, Count of Léon. Thanks to the ducal treasury, he recruited mercenaries which allowed him to perform in June and July a 'great ride in Brittany' (as described by Arthur de la Borderie) and take control of the duchy. John first gained [Rennes](https://alchetron.com/Rennes), then [Vannes](https://alchetron.com/Vannes) and the places surrounding the [Château de Suscinio](https://alchetron.com/Ch%C3%A2teau-de-Suscinio), [Auray](https://alchetron.com/Auray), Hennebont, and then Quimperlé. Having failed to take the domains of [Rohan](https://alchetron.com/House-of-Rohan), he submitted [Quimper](https://alchetron.com/Quimper) and [Brest](https://alchetron.com/Brest%2C-France) before descending to Carhaix, and then went back northward and captured [Saint-Brieuc](https://alchetron.com/Saint-Brieuc), [Lamballe](https://alchetron.com/Lamballe), Jugon, [Dinan](https://alchetron.com/Dinan), [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://alchetron.com/Dol-de-Bretagne), and returned to Nantes via [Ploërmel](https://alchetron.com/Plo%C3%ABrmel).

Always accompanied by Hervé VII of Léon, John obtained the submission, if not the support, of some of the major nobles who possessed several of these strongholds and had been loyal to Charles of Blois. However it would probably require getting [Josselin](https://alchetron.com/Josselin), or the support of the high secular clergy and great lords, or more, to control the domains of the Penthièvres and the House of Rohan, which represented about two-thirds of Brittany. John also went to England and met with Edward III of England in Windsor, who promised him military assistance and invested him with the [Honour of Richmond](https://alchetron.com/Honour-of-Richmond).

Charles of Blois then made an appeal to Philip VI, who summoned John of Montfort to a Court of Peers session in Conflans in September 1341. In this context by the judgment of Conflans, the Duchy of Brittany was attributed to Charles of Blois. Philip VI agreed to receive _l'hommage lige_ of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, and confiscated from John of Montfort the French lands of the County of Montfort-l'Amaury, as well as the Viscounty of Limoges that he held more unduly.

In October 1341, Charles of Blois and [John II, Duke of Normandy](https://alchetron.com/John-II-of-France) (later King of France), put together an army and penetrated into Brittany. They managed to retrieve a number of strongholds which had been lost, including Nantes, which relented on 21 November 1341 after three weeks of siege. John of Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://alchetron.com/Louvre) in Paris. Despite the change of camp of Hervé VII de Leon (due to criticisms from John regarding his handling of the siege of Nantes), Joanna, the wife of John of Montfort, continued the armed struggle supported by his allies.

After a winter break that ended on 15 April 1342, Charles of Blois resumed the fight and regained a large part of Brittany between May and September 1342. King Edward III of England decided to intervene on behalf of the House of Montfort. Charles de Blois failed to take Hennebont, which was defended by Joanna of Flanders, while [Robert III of Artois](https://alchetron.com/Robert-III-of-Artois) was mortally wounded besieging Vannes in vain leading an English contingent. In January 1343, through [Pope Clement VI](https://alchetron.com/Pope-Clement-VI), a truce was signed at [Malestroit](https://alchetron.com/Malestroit) to bring peace and the liberation of John of Montfort. The latter was released in September 1343 and retired to England 27 March 1345. His return to the struggle with reinforcements provided by King Edward III of England put an end to the truce. John of Montfort unsuccessfully laid siege to Quimper, then fell ill and died in Hennebont on 26 September 1345.

He was buried in the convent of the Dominicans of Quimperlé where his tomb, which had already been desecrated, was found again in December 1883. His remains are now in the Church of Sainte-Croix de Quimperlé.

**John IV (or V)** (born _c._ 1340—died Nov. 1, 1399, [Nantes](https://www.britannica.com/place/Nantes), Fr.) was the [duke](https://www.britannica.com/topic/duke) of Brittany from 1365, whose support for English interests during the [Hundred Years’ War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Hundred-Years-War) (1337–1453) nearly cost him the [forfeit](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/forfeit) of his duchy to the French crown. The instability of his reign is attributable not only to his alliances with England but also to his imposition of harsh taxes on his subjects.

John was educated at the court of King [Edward III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-III-king-of-England) of England. He ended the [War of the Breton Succession](https://www.britannica.com/event/War-of-the-Breton-Succession) in September 1364 by defeating [Charles of Blois](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-duke-of-Brittany) at Auray; he was recognized as duke of Brittany by King [Charles V](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-V-king-of-France) of [France](https://www.britannica.com/place/France) in the [Treaty of Guérande](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Guerande) (April 12, 1365). John secretly aided Edward’s cause in 1370, giving the English soldier Robert Knowles a haven in Brittany when Knowles faced defeat at the hands of French forces. In 1372, after making an alliance with Edward, John was granted the earldom of Richmond for allowing the English to garrison his [fortresses](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/fortresses) in Brittany.

After the French drove the English from most of the duchy, however, John fled to England (April 1373). Charles’s confiscation of John’s property in 1378 met with condemnation from the people of Brittany, but John lost this support when he made an alliance with King [Richard II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Richard-II-king-of-England) of England in 1380. He managed to reverse his loss by making peace with the regents for King [Charles VI](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-VI-king-of-France) through the second Treaty of Guérande (Jan. 15, 1381). In 1392 he was again in ill repute with the crown for instigating an assassination attempt on Charles VI’s constable of France, [Olivier de Clisson](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Olivier-de-Clisson), with whom he had had a long personal feud.
